claim: Volume-regulated anion channels (VRACs) mediate volume regulatory Cl- and organic solute efflux from vertebrate cells.
source: Volume-regulated anion channels (VRACs) mediate volume regulatory Cl- and organic solute efflux from vertebrate cells.
evidence: This is a statement about the function of VRACs supported by established scientific knowledge in the field.

claim: VRACs are heteromeric assemblies of LRRC8A-E proteins with unknown stoichiometries.
source: VRACs are heteromeric assemblies of LRRC8A-E proteins with unknown stoichiometries.
evidence: This statement reflects established knowledge about VRAC composition while acknowledging the unknown stoichiometry.

claim: Homomeric LRRC8A and LRRC8D channels have a small pore, hexameric structure.
source: Homomeric LRRC8A and LRRC8D channels have a small pore, hexameric structure.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous structural studies mentioned in the manuscript.

claim: Homomeric LRRC8A and LRRC8D channels are either non-functional or exhibit abnormal regulation and pharmacology.
source: However, these channels are either non-functional or exhibit abnormal regulation and pharmacology, limiting their utility for structure-function analyses.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous functional studies.

claim: The LRRC8C-LRRC8A(IL125) chimera comprises LRRC8C and 25 amino acids unique to the first intracellular loop (IL1) of LRRC8A.
source: We demonstrate here that the LRRC8C-LRRC8A(IL125) chimera comprising LRRC8C and 25 amino acids unique to the first intracellular loop (IL1) of LRRC8A has a heptameric structure like that of homologous pannexin channels.
evidence: This is a direct description of the chimera construct design.

claim: The LRRC8C-LRRC8A(IL125) chimera has a heptameric structure.
source: We demonstrate here that the LRRC8C-LRRC8A(IL125) chimera comprising LRRC8C and 25 amino acids unique to the first intracellular loop (IL1) of LRRC8A has a heptameric structure like that of homologous pannexin channels.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by cryo-EM structural data.

claim: The heptameric structure of LRRC8C-LRRC8A(IL125) is like that of homologous pannexin channels.
source: We demonstrate here that the LRRC8C-LRRC8A(IL125) chimera comprising LRRC8C and 25 amino acids unique to the first intracellular loop (IL1) of LRRC8A has a heptameric structure like that of homologous pannexin channels.
evidence: This comparison is based on structural similarity to known pannexin structures.

claim: Heptameric LRRC8C-LRRC8A(IL125) channels have a large-diameter pore similar to that estimated for native VRACs.
source: Unlike homomeric LRRC8A and LRRC8D channels, heptameric LRRC8C-LRRC8A(IL125) channels have a large-diameter pore similar to that estimated for native VRACs, exhibit normal DCPIB pharmacology, and have higher permeability to large organic anions.
evidence: This claim is supported by structural measurements and comparison to literature values for native VRACs.

claim: Heptameric LRRC8C-LRRC8A(IL125) channels exhibit normal DCPIB pharmacology.
source: Unlike homomeric LRRC8A and LRRC8D channels, heptameric LRRC8C-LRRC8A(IL125) channels have a large-diameter pore similar to that estimated for native VRACs, exhibit normal DCPIB pharmacology, and have higher permeability to large organic anions.
evidence: This is supported by functional data comparing the chimera to native channels.

claim: Heptameric LRRC8C-LRRC8A(IL125) channels have higher permeability to large organic anions than homomeric LRRC8A and LRRC8D channels.
source: Unlike homomeric LRRC8A and LRRC8D channels, heptameric LRRC8C-LRRC8A(IL125) channels have a large-diameter pore similar to that estimated for native VRACs, exhibit normal DCPIB pharmacology, and have higher permeability to large organic anions.
evidence: This is supported by permeability measurements presented in the manuscript.

claim: Lipid-like densities are located between LRRC8C-LRRC8A(IL125) subunits.
source: Lipid-like densities are located between LRRC8C-LRRC8A(IL125) subunits and occlude the channel pore.
evidence: This is based on cryo-EM density observations.

claim: Lipid-like densities occlude the channel pore of LRRC8C-LRRC8A(IL125).
source: Lipid-like densities are located between LRRC8C-LRRC8A(IL125) subunits and occlude the channel pore.
evidence: This is based on cryo-EM density observations.

claim: Lipids may play important roles in VRAC/LRRC8 channel gating and regulation.
source: Our findings provide new insights into VRAC/LRRC8 channel structure and suggest that lipids may play important roles in channel gating and regulation.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation based on the observed lipid densities.

claim: VRACs are activated by increases in cell volume.
source: VRACs are activated by increases in cell volume and by large reductions in intracellular ionic strength (Strange et al., 2019).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: VRACs are activated by large reductions in intracellular ionic strength.
source: VRACs are activated by increases in cell volume and by large reductions in intracellular ionic strength (Strange et al., 2019).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: VRACs are encoded by the Lrrc8 gene family.
source: VRACs are encoded by the Lrrc8 gene family (Qiu et al., 2014; Voss et al., 2014), which comprises five paralogs termed Lrrc8a-e (Abascal and Zardoya, 2012; Voss et al., 2014).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: The Lrrc8 gene family comprises five paralogs termed Lrrc8a-e.
source: VRACs are encoded by the Lrrc8 gene family (Qiu et al., 2014; Voss et al., 2014), which comprises five paralogs termed Lrrc8a-e (Abascal and Zardoya, 2012; Voss et al., 2014).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Native VRAC/LRRC8 channels are heteromers with unknown stoichiometry.
source: Native VRAC/LRRC8 channels are heteromers with unknown stoichiometry.
evidence: This reflects current knowledge about VRAC composition.

claim: LRRC8A is an essential VRAC/LRRC8 subunit.
source: LRRC8A is an essential VRAC/LRRC8 subunit and must be co-expressed with at least one other paralog to reconstitute volume-regulated channel activity (Syeda et al., 2016; Voss et al., 2014).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: LRRC8A must be co-expressed with at least one other paralog to reconstitute volume-regulated channel activity.
source: LRRC8A is an essential VRAC/LRRC8 subunit and must be co-expressed with at least one other paralog to reconstitute volume-regulated channel activity (Syeda et al., 2016; Voss et al., 2014).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: High-resolution cryo-EM structures have been determined for homomeric LRRC8A channels.
source: High-resolution cryo-electron microscopy (cryo-EM) structures have been determined for homomeric LRRC8A (Deneka et al., 2021; Deneka et al., 2018; Kasuya et al., 2018; Kefauver et al., 2018; Kern et al., 2019) and LRRC8D (Nakamura et al., 2020) channels demonstrating that they have a hexameric configuration.
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous structural studies.

claim: High-resolution cryo-EM structures have been determined for homomeric LRRC8D channels.
source: High-resolution cryo-electron microscopy (cryo-EM) structures have been determined for homomeric LRRC8A (Deneka et al., 2021; Deneka et al., 2018; Kasuya et al., 2018; Kefauver et al., 2018; Kern et al., 2019) and LRRC8D (Nakamura et al., 2020) channels demonstrating that they have a hexameric configuration.
evidence: This is supported by citation to a previous structural study.

claim: Homomeric LRRC8A channels have a hexameric configuration.
source: High-resolution cryo-electron microscopy (cryo-EM) structures have been determined for homomeric LRRC8A (Deneka et al., 2021; Deneka et al., 2018; Kasuya et al., 2018; Kefauver et al., 2018; Kern et al., 2019) and LRRC8D (Nakamura et al., 2020) channels demonstrating that they have a hexameric configuration.
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous structural studies.

claim: Homomeric LRRC8D channels have a hexameric configuration.
source: High-resolution cryo-electron microscopy (cryo-EM) structures have been determined for homomeric LRRC8A (Deneka et al., 2021; Deneka et al., 2018; Kasuya et al., 2018; Kefauver et al., 2018; Kern et al., 2019) and LRRC8D (Nakamura et al., 2020) channels demonstrating that they have a hexameric configuration.
evidence: This is supported by citation to a previous structural study.

claim: Homomeric LRRC8A channels have abnormal functional properties.
source: Homomeric LRRC8A and LRRC8D channels have abnormal functional properties or are not expressed in the plasma membrane (Voss et al., 2014; Yamada et al., 2021; Yamada and Strange, 2018; Zhou et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous functional studies.

claim: Homomeric LRRC8D channels are not expressed in the plasma membrane.
source: Homomeric LRRC8A and LRRC8D channels have abnormal functional properties or are not expressed in the plasma membrane (Voss et al., 2014; Yamada et al., 2021; Yamada and Strange, 2018; Zhou et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous functional studies.

claim: Structure-function studies of VRAC/LRRC8 heteromeric channels are complicated by their undefined, likely variable, and experimentally uncontrollable stoichiometry.
source: Structure-function studies of VRAC/LRRC8 heteromeric channels are complicated by their undefined, likely variable, and experimentally uncontrollable stoichiometry.
evidence: This is an inference based on the nature of heteromeric channel assembly.

claim: Novel homomeric LRRC8 chimeras exhibit functional properties similar to native heteromeric VRAC/LRRC8 channels.
source: To circumvent these problems, we developed a series of novel homomeric LRRC8 chimeras that exhibit functional properties similar to the native heteromeric VRAC/LRRC8 channels (Yamada and Strange, 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: 8C-8A(IL125) consists of a 25-amino acid sequence unique to the first intracellular loop, IL1, of LRRC8A inserted into the corresponding region of LRRC8C.
source: 8C-8A(IL125) consists of a 25-amino acid sequence unique to the first intracellular loop, IL1, of LRRC8A inserted into the corresponding region of LRRC8C (Figure 1).
evidence: This is a description of the chimera construct design, illustrated in Figure 1.

claim: 8C-8A(IL125) chimeras are activated strongly by cell swelling.
source: Like native VRAC/LRRC8 channels, 8C-8A(IL125) chimeras are activated strongly by cell swelling and low intracellular ionic strength (Yamada and Strange, 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a previous functional study.

claim: 8C-8A(IL125) chimeras are activated strongly by low intracellular ionic strength.
source: Like native VRAC/LRRC8 channels, 8C-8A(IL125) chimeras are activated strongly by cell swelling and low intracellular ionic strength (Yamada and Strange, 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a previous functional study.

claim: The 8C-8A(IL125) chimeric channel is a large-pore seven-subunit heptamer.
source: We demonstrate that the 8C-8A(IL125) chimeric channel is a large-pore seven-subunit heptamer, like homologous pannexin channels (Bhat and Sajjad, 2021; Deng et al., 2020; Jin et al., 2020; Kuzuya et al., 2022; Michalski et al., 2020; Mou et al., 2020; Qu et al., 2020; Ruan et al., 2020).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by cryo-EM data and comparison to pannexin structures.

claim: The pore diameter of 8C-8A(IL125) is similar to that estimated for native VRACs.
source: The pore diameter is similar to that estimated for native VRACs, and permeability to large organic anions is significantly higher than that of homohexameric LRRC8A channels.
evidence: This is supported by structural measurements and comparison to literature values.

claim: Permeability to large organic anions is significantly higher in 8C-8A(IL125) than in homohexameric LRRC8A channels.
source: The pore diameter is similar to that estimated for native VRACs, and permeability to large organic anions is significantly higher than that of homohexameric LRRC8A channels.
evidence: This is supported by permeability measurements presented in the manuscript.

claim: Lipid-like densities occlude the channel pore in 8C-8A(IL125), as has been shown recently for human pannexin 1.
source: Lipid-like densities are located between 8C-8A(IL125) channel subunits and occlude the channel pore, as has been shown recently for human pannexin 1 (Kuzuya et al., 2022).
evidence: This is based on cryo-EM observations and comparison to a recent pannexin study.

claim: LRRC8 proteins can form anion channels with different subunit numbers.
source: Our results, together with the previous studies (Deneka et al., 2021; Deneka et al., 2018; Kasuya et al., 2018; Kefauver et al., 2018; Kern et al., 2019; Nakamura et al., 2020), demonstrate that LRRC8 proteins can form anion channels with different subunit numbers.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the current study's data and previous structural studies.

claim: Leucine-rich repeat motifs play essential roles in signal transduction.
source: Leucine-rich repeat motifs have been identified in over 14,000 proteins from viruses to eukaryotes and play essential roles in signal transduction and as sites for protein-protein interactions (Bella et al., 2008; Kobe and Kajava, 2001; Matsushima et al., 2019).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Leucine-rich repeat motifs serve as sites for protein-protein interactions.
source: Leucine-rich repeat motifs have been identified in over 14,000 proteins from viruses to eukaryotes and play essential roles in signal transduction and as sites for protein-protein interactions (Bella et al., 2008; Kobe and Kajava, 2001; Matsushima et al., 2019).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: The LRR motif can function as a mechanosensor.
source: The LRR motif can also function as a mechanosensor (Ju et al., 2016; Ju et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: VRAC/LRRC8 channels most likely arose by fusion of the transmembrane domain encoding portion of a pannexin channel gene with the LRRD portion of an unrelated gene type.
source: VRAC/LRRC8 channels most likely arose by fusion of the transmembrane domain encoding portion of a pannexin channel gene with the LRRD portion of an unrelated gene type (Abascal and Zardoya, 2012).
evidence: This is an evolutionary hypothesis supported by citation.

claim: Conformational changes in the VRAC/LRRC8 channel LRR domain are correlated with changes in channel activity.
source: Conformational changes in the VRAC/LRRC8 channel LRR domain are correlated with changes in channel activity (Deneka et al., 2021; König et al., 2019), and multiple cryo-EM structures demonstrate that this region is conformationally flexible (Figure 5; Deneka et al., 2021; Deneka et al., 2018; Kasuya et al., 2018; Kefauver et al., 2018; Kern et al., 2019; Nakamura et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies and data from the current study (Figure 5).

claim: The VRAC/LRRC8 channel LRRD is conformationally flexible.
source: Conformational changes in the VRAC/LRRC8 channel LRR domain are correlated with changes in channel activity (Deneka et al., 2021; König et al., 2019), and multiple cryo-EM structures demonstrate that this region is conformationally flexible (Figure 5; Deneka et al., 2021; Deneka et al., 2018; Kasuya et al., 2018; Kefauver et al., 2018; Kern et al., 2019; Nakamura et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies and data from the current study (Figure 5).

claim: The VRAC/LRRC8 channel LRRD is likely a critical element of the channel's cell volume sensing apparatus.
source: These data all point to the high likelihood that the VRAC/LRRC8 channel LRRD is a critical element of the channel's cell volume sensing apparatus.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observed conformational flexibility and correlation with channel activity.

claim: LRRC8 chimeras with normal cell volume and ionic strength sensitivity must contain all or part of the LRRC8A IL1.
source: LRRC8 chimeras with normal cell volume and ionic strength sensitivity must contain all or part of the LRRC8A IL1 (Yamada and Strange, 2018), indicating that this protein region is also critical for channel regulation.
evidence: This is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: The LRRC8A IL1 region is critical for channel regulation.
source: LRRC8 chimeras with normal cell volume and ionic strength sensitivity must contain all or part of the LRRC8A IL1 (Yamada and Strange, 2018), indicating that this protein region is also critical for channel regulation.
evidence: This is an inference based on the requirement for IL1 in functional chimeras.

claim: The 25-amino acid region of the LRRC8A IL1 inserted into the 8C-8A(IL125) chimera is predicted to be intrinsically disordered.
source: The 25-amino acid region of the LRRC8A IL1 inserted into the 8C-8A(IL125) chimera is predicted to be intrinsically disordered (Yamada and Strange, 2018).
evidence: This is a prediction supported by citation.

claim: The 25-amino acid region of the LRRC8A IL1 was not visible in the cryo-EM structures.
source: Consistent with this prediction, this region was not visible in our cryo-EM structures.
evidence: This is an observation from the cryo-EM data.

claim: The LRRC8A IL1 may be required for correct channel assembly and conformation.
source: It is conceivable that the LRRC8A IL1 is required for correct channel assembly and conformation, that it plays a direct role in cell volume sensing and/or that it functions to transduce cell volume-induced conformational changes into changes in the gating.
evidence: This is speculation about the possible roles of IL1.

claim: The LRRC8A IL1 may play a direct role in cell volume sensing.
source: It is conceivable that the LRRC8A IL1 is required for correct channel assembly and conformation, that it plays a direct role in cell volume sensing and/or that it functions to transduce cell volume-induced conformational changes into changes in the gating.
evidence: This is speculation about the possible roles of IL1.

claim: The LRRC8A IL1 may function to transduce cell volume-induced conformational changes into changes in gating.
source: It is conceivable that the LRRC8A IL1 is required for correct channel assembly and conformation, that it plays a direct role in cell volume sensing and/or that it functions to transduce cell volume-induced conformational changes into changes in the gating.
evidence: This is speculation about the possible roles of IL1.

claim: The purified 8C-8A(IL125) complex appeared larger than the LRRC8A hexamers in native-PAGE.
source: The purified 8C-8A(IL125) complex appeared larger than the LRRC8A hexamers in both native-PAGE and size exclusion chromatography analysis (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B–C).
evidence: This is an observation from biochemical analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: The purified 8C-8A(IL125) complex appeared larger than the LRRC8A hexamers in size exclusion chromatography.
source: The purified 8C-8A(IL125) complex appeared larger than the LRRC8A hexamers in both native-PAGE and size exclusion chromatography analysis (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B–C).
evidence: This is an observation from biochemical analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Five distinct 3D classes were obtained for 8C-8A(IL125) after 3D classification.
source: Following 2D classification and ab initio 3D reconstruction, we performed 3D classification and obtained five distinct 3D classes for 8C-8A(IL125) (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a result from cryo-EM data processing shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: The 8C-8A(IL125) maps showed no apparent symmetric arrangement.
source: The 8C-8A(IL125) maps showed no apparent symmetric arrangement.
evidence: This is an observation from the cryo-EM maps.

claim: The final reconstructions of 8C-8A(IL125) were done without enforcing any symmetry.
source: Therefore, the final reconstructions were done without enforcing any symmetry and resulted in five structures with resolutions in the range of 3.4–4.0 Å (Figure 2A and B, Figure 2—figure supplements 1 and 2, and Table 1).
evidence: This is a description of the data processing method.

claim: Five structures of 8C-8A(IL125) were obtained with resolutions in the range of 3.4–4.0 Å.
source: Therefore, the final reconstructions were done without enforcing any symmetry and resulted in five structures with resolutions in the range of 3.4–4.0 Å (Figure 2A and B, Figure 2—figure supplements 1 and 2, and Table 1).
evidence: This is a result from cryo-EM data processing.

claim: The 8C-8A(IL125) structure comprises four domains: ECD, TMD, ICD, and LRRD.
source: Similar to LRRC8A and LRRC8D structures, the 8C-8A(IL125) structure comprises four domains, the extracellular domain (ECD), transmembrane domain (TMD), intracellular domain (ICD), and leucine-rich repeat (LRR) motif-containing domain (LRRD) (Figure 2).
evidence: This is a structural description based on cryo-EM data shown in Figure 2.

claim: An atomic model was built comprising most of the ECD and TMD except residues 60–94 in the ECD and the first 15 residues of the N-terminus.
source: The cryo-EM maps for the ECD and TMD revealed high-resolution features allowing us to build an atomic model comprising most of the ECD and TMD except residues 60–94 in the ECD and the first 15 residues of the N-terminus.
evidence: This is a description of the model building process.

claim: The first intracellular loop containing the swapped IL125 region remained unresolved in the cryo-EM maps.
source: However, the first intracellular loop containing the swapped IL125 region remained unresolved.
evidence: This is an observation from the cryo-EM data.

claim: The local resolution for the LRRD was insufficient to build an atomic model.
source: Although the unsharpened maps revealed clear features for the entire protein, the local resolution for the LRRD was insufficient to build an atomic model, and the local refinement strategy we applied did not provide any meaningful improvement in LRRD resolution (Figure 2A–E and Figure 2—figure supplements 1 and 2).
evidence: This is an observation from the cryo-EM data processing.

claim: The overall structure of an individual 8C-8A(IL125) subunit is similar to that of LRRC8A.
source: The overall structure of an individual 8C-8A(IL125) subunit is similar to that of LRRC8A (Figure 2F) and LRRC8D.
evidence: This is a structural comparison shown in Figure 2F.

claim: The overall structure of an individual 8C-8A(IL125) subunit is similar to that of LRRC8D.
source: The overall structure of an individual 8C-8A(IL125) subunit is similar to that of LRRC8A (Figure 2F) and LRRC8D.
evidence: This is a structural comparison.

claim: The 8C-8A(IL125) chimeric channel is a seven-subunit heptamer, similar to homologous pannexin channels.
source: However, unlike homomeric LRRC8A and LRRC8D channels, which are hexamers (Deneka et al., 2021; Deneka et al., 2018; Kasuya et al., 2018; Kefauver et al., 2018; Kern et al., 2019; Nakamura et al., 2020), the 8C-8A(IL125) chimeric channel is a seven-subunit heptamer, similar to the homologous pannexin channels (Figure 2B and E; Figure 2—figure supplement 3; Bhat and Sajjad, 2021; Deng et al., 2020; Jin et al., 2020; Kuzuya et al., 2022; Michalski et al., 2020; Mou et al., 2020; Qu et al., 2020; Ruan et al., 2020).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by cryo-EM data and comparison to pannexin structures.

claim: The subunit arrangement of the 8C-8A(IL125) heptameric channel is asymmetric.
source: The subunit arrangement of the 8C-8A(IL125) heptameric channel is asymmetric as opposed to LRRC8A and LRRC8D hexamers, which have two-, three-, or sixfold symmetric arrangements (Deneka et al., 2021; Deneka et al., 2018; Kasuya et al., 2018; Kefauver et al., 2018; Kern et al., 2019; Nakamura et al., 2020).
evidence: This is an observation from the cryo-EM structure.

claim: LRRC8A and LRRC8D hexamers have two-, three-, or sixfold symmetric arrangements.
source: The subunit arrangement of the 8C-8A(IL125) heptameric channel is asymmetric as opposed to LRRC8A and LRRC8D hexamers, which have two-, three-, or sixfold symmetric arrangements (Deneka et al., 2021; Deneka et al., 2018; Kasuya et al., 2018; Kefauver et al., 2018; Kern et al., 2019; Nakamura et al., 2020).
evidence: This is established knowledge from previous structural studies.

claim: 8C-8A(IL125) subunits are organized into two distinct groups when viewed from the cytoplasm: one with four subunits and the other with three subunits.
source: When the ICD and TMD are viewed from the cytoplasm, 8C-8A(IL125) subunits are organized into two distinct groups, one with four subunits and the other with three subunits (Figure 3A–D).
evidence: This is an observation from the cryo-EM structure shown in Figure 3.

claim: The two groups of subunits in 8C-8A(IL125) associate via a loose interface.
source: These two groups of subunits associate via a loose interface, while the subunits within each group associate via a tight interface (Figure 3A–D and Figure 3—figure supplements 1–3).
evidence: This is an observation from the cryo-EM structure shown in Figure 3.

claim: The subunits within each group in 8C-8A(IL125) associate via a tight interface.
source: These two groups of subunits associate via a loose interface, while the subunits within each group associate via a tight interface (Figure 3A–D and Figure 3—figure supplements 1–3).
evidence: This is an observation from the cryo-EM structure shown in Figure 3.

claim: The ECDs of 8C-8A(IL125) are arranged symmetrically.
source: In contrast to the ICDs and TMDs, the ECDs are arranged symmetrically and form extensive contacts between the subunits in both tight and loose interfaces (Figure 3E and Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is an observation from the cryo-EM structure shown in Figure 3.

claim: The ECDs of 8C-8A(IL125) form extensive contacts between the subunits in both tight and loose interfaces.
source: In contrast to the ICDs and TMDs, the ECDs are arranged symmetrically and form extensive contacts between the subunits in both tight and loose interfaces (Figure 3E and Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is an observation from the cryo-EM structure shown in Figure 3.

claim: Most of the subunit interaction in the ECD is between residues on ELH1 and the linker connecting EL2β1 and EL2β2 in one subunit and residues on the three β-strands of the neighboring subunit.
source: Most of the subunit interaction is between the residues on ELH1 and the linker that connects EL2β1 and EL2β2 in one subunit and the residues on the three β-strands of the neighboring subunit (Figure 3E and Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a detailed structural observation from the cryo-EM structure.

claim: The contacts between each subunit pair bury about 1900 Å2 of solvent-accessible surface area at the ECDs.
source: The contacts between each subunit pair bury about 1900 Å2 of solvent-accessible surface area at the ECDs (Table 2).
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from structural analysis shown in Table 2.

claim: The buried solvent-accessible surface areas between subunit pairs in the TMDs and ICDs are considerably smaller than in the ECDs.
source: The buried solvent-accessible surface areas between the subunit pairs in the TMDs and ICDs are considerably smaller and exhibit high variability between the tight and the loose interfaces.
evidence: This is a quantitative observation from structural analysis.

claim: The buried areas in the TMD are about 650 and 110 Å2 for the tight and loose interfaces, respectively.
source: In the TMD, the buried areas are about 650 and 110 Å2 for the tight and loose interfaces, respectively (Table 2).
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from structural analysis shown in Table 2.

claim: In the ICD, the buried areas in the tight interfaces range from 290 to 560 Å2.
source: In the ICD, the buried areas in the tight interfaces range from 290 to 560 Å2, whereas there are no solvent-inaccessible contacts at the loose interfaces (Figure 3E, Figure 3—figure supplements 2–3, and Table 2).
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from structural analysis shown in Table 2.

claim: There are no solvent-inaccessible contacts at the loose interfaces in the ICD.
source: In the ICD, the buried areas in the tight interfaces range from 290 to 560 Å2, whereas there are no solvent-inaccessible contacts at the loose interfaces (Figure 3E, Figure 3—figure supplements 2–3, and Table 2).
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from structural analysis shown in Table 2.

claim: The asymmetric arrangement of TMDs and ICDs is likely due to their divergent orientation relative to the ECDs.
source: The asymmetric arrangement observed for the TMDs and ICDs is likely due to their divergent orientation relative to the ECDs.
evidence: This is an inference based on structural observations.

claim: TMDs exhibit up to an 8° difference in their orientation relative to the ECD.
source: Figure 4A shows the alignment of the seven subunits on their ECDs. TMDs do not align and exhibit up to an 8° difference in their orientation relative to the ECD, while the difference is larger for the ICDs (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from structural analysis shown in Figure 4A.

claim: The difference in orientation relative to the ECD is larger for the ICDs than for the TMDs.
source: Figure 4A shows the alignment of the seven subunits on their ECDs. TMDs do not align and exhibit up to an 8° difference in their orientation relative to the ECD, while the difference is larger for the ICDs (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is a qualitative observation from structural analysis shown in Figure 4A.

claim: In two of the subunits in the class 1 structure, K51 points toward the pore while D50 points in the opposite direction.
source: In two of the subunits in the class 1 structure, K51 points toward the pore, while D50 points in the opposite direction. In the five other subunits, D50 points toward the pore, and K51 is oriented toward the subunit interface (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is a detailed structural observation from the cryo-EM structure shown in Figure 4C.

claim: In five of the subunits in the class 1 structure, D50 points toward the pore and K51 is oriented toward the subunit interface.
source: In two of the subunits in the class 1 structure, K51 points toward the pore, while D50 points in the opposite direction. In the five other subunits, D50 points toward the pore, and K51 is oriented toward the subunit interface (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is a detailed structural observation from the cryo-EM structure shown in Figure 4C.

claim: When K51 points toward the pore, it creates a groove between the subunits.
source: When K51 points toward the pore, it creates a groove between the subunits (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is a structural observation from the cryo-EM structure shown in Figure 4D.

claim: The grooves created by K51 pointing toward the pore are located between the subunits forming the loose interface in the class 1 structure.
source: These grooves, located between the subunits forming the loose interface in the class 1 structure, connect the space within the ECD to the membrane-facing surface of the TMD (Figure 4E).
evidence: This is a structural observation from the cryo-EM structure shown in Figure 4E.

claim: The grooves connect the space within the ECD to the membrane-facing surface of the TMD.
source: These grooves, located between the subunits forming the loose interface in the class 1 structure, connect the space within the ECD to the membrane-facing surface of the TMD (Figure 4E).
evidence: This is a structural observation from the cryo-EM structure shown in Figure 4E.

claim: When D50 points toward the pore, the side chain of K51 occupies the groove space, closing the groove.
source: When D50 points toward the pore, the side chain of K51 occupies this space, closing the groove (Figure 4F).
evidence: This is a structural observation from the cryo-EM structure shown in Figure 4F.

claim: The most apparent difference between the five 3D classes is in the arrangement of the LRRDs.
source: We obtained five distinct 3D classes for the 8C-8A(IL125) chimera. The most apparent difference between the structures is in the arrangement of the LRRDs (Figure 5A–B).
evidence: This is an observation from the cryo-EM data shown in Figure 5.

claim: In class 1, all seven LRRDs are arranged circularly with roughly sevenfold symmetry.
source: In class 1, all seven LRRDs are arranged circularly with roughly sevenfold symmetry.
evidence: This is a structural observation from the cryo-EM structure.

claim: For class 5, one of the LRRDs is positioned outside of the quaternary assembly formed by six LRRDs arranged with pseudo-twofold symmetry.
source: For class 5, one of the LRRDs is positioned outside of the quaternary assembly formed by six LRRDs arranged with pseudo-twofold symmetry.
evidence: This is a structural observation from the cryo-EM structure.

claim: The density for the LRRD located outside the assembly in class 5 is poorly visible, indicating high flexibility relative to the rest of the complex.
source: The density for the LRRD located outside the assembly is poorly visible, indicating high flexibility relative to the rest of the complex (Figure 5A–B).
evidence: This is an inference based on the quality of the cryo-EM density shown in Figure 5.

claim: The ICDs exhibit conformational heterogeneity among the five 3D classes.
source: Consistent with the conformational differences in the arrangements of the LRRDs, the ICDs also exhibit conformational heterogeneity, albeit less pronounced, among the five 3D classes we observed (Figure 5C and Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is an observation from the cryo-EM structures shown in Figure 5.

claim: The distances between the subunits forming the tight interfaces appear similar in all classes.
source: The distances between the subunits forming the tight interfaces appear similar in all classes, whereas the distances between the subunits forming the loose interfaces are variable among different classes.
evidence: This is an observation from the cryo-EM structures.

claim: The distances between the subunits forming the loose interfaces are variable among different classes.
source: The distances between the subunits forming the tight interfaces appear similar in all classes, whereas the distances between the subunits forming the loose interfaces are variable among different classes.
evidence: This is an observation from the cryo-EM structures.

claim: A similar variation in subunit distances is observed within the TMD among different classes.
source: A similar variation is also observed within the TMD (Figure 5D and Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is an observation from the cryo-EM structures shown in Figure 5.

claim: There are no apparent structural differences at the ECD of the structures among different classes.
source: However, there are no apparent structural differences at the ECD of the structures (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is an observation from the cryo-EM structures shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: The number of subunits with K51 pointing toward the pores differs among classes.
source: The distinct arrangement of the loops formed by D50 and K51 is also observed in other classes (Figure 5—figure supplement 2). However, the number of subunits with K51 pointing toward the pores differs.
evidence: This is an observation from the cryo-EM structures shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claim: The class 2 structure has only one subunit with K51 pointing toward the pore, compared to two subunits in the class 1 structure.
source: For example, the class 2 structure has only one subunit with K51 pointing toward the pore, compared to two subunits in the class 1 structure (Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is a specific observation from the cryo-EM structures shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claim: The narrowest region of the heptameric 8C-8A(IL125) channel pore has an average solvent-accessible radius of 4.7 Å.
source: The narrowest region of the heptameric 8C-8A(IL125) channel pore has an average solvent-accessible radius of 4.7 Å and is formed by L105 located on the extracellular side of the protein (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from structural analysis shown in Figure 6A.

claim: The narrowest region of the heptameric 8C-8A(IL125) channel pore is formed by L105 located on the extracellular side of the protein.
source: The narrowest region of the heptameric 8C-8A(IL125) channel pore has an average solvent-accessible radius of 4.7 Å and is formed by L105 located on the extracellular side of the protein (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is a structural observation from the cryo-EM structure shown in Figure 6A.

claim: The pore radius of 4.7 Å in 8C-8A(IL125) is considerably larger than the pore radius of 2.0 Å in hexameric LRRC8A channels.
source: This is considerably larger than the pore radius of 2.0 Å determined from cryo-EM structures of hexameric LRRC8A channels (Figure 6B–C; Deneka et al., 2018; Kasuya et al., 2018; Kefauver et al., 2018; Kern et al., 2019).
evidence: This is a quantitative comparison based on structural measurements shown in Figure 6.

claim: The pore radius of hexameric LRRC8A channels is 2.0 Å.
source: This is considerably larger than the pore radius of 2.0 Å determined from cryo-EM structures of hexameric LRRC8A channels (Figure 6B–C; Deneka et al., 2018; Kasuya et al., 2018; Kefauver et al., 2018; Kern et al., 2019).
evidence: This is a measurement from previous structural studies.

claim: The difference in pore diameters of hexameric LRRC8A channels and heptameric 8C-8A(IL125) channels implies that subunit number impacts channel solute permeability.
source: The difference in pore diameters of hexameric LRRC8A channels and heptameric 8C-8A(IL125) channels implies that subunit number impacts channel solute permeability.
evidence: This is an inference based on the structural differences.

claim: Pglutathione/PCl is significantly higher for the 8C-8A(IL125) heptameric channel than for LRRC8A.
source: Pglutathione/PCl and Plactobionate/PCl were both significantly (p<0.01) higher for the 8C-8A(IL125) heptameric channel (Figure 6D–E), consistent with its larger pore diameter.
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from permeability experiments shown in Figure 6D-E.

claim: Plactobionate/PCl is significantly higher for the 8C-8A(IL125) heptameric channel than for LRRC8A.
source: Pglutathione/PCl and Plactobionate/PCl were both significantly (p<0.01) higher for the 8C-8A(IL125) heptameric channel (Figure 6D–E), consistent with its larger pore diameter.
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from permeability experiments shown in Figure 6D-E.

claim: The higher permeability to large organic anions in 8C-8A(IL125) is consistent with its larger pore diameter.
source: Pglutathione/PCl and Plactobionate/PCl were both significantly (p<0.01) higher for the 8C-8A(IL125) heptameric channel (Figure 6D–E), consistent with its larger pore diameter.
evidence: This is an inference connecting the structural and functional data.

claim: Non-protein densities penetrate through the openings between the subunits in the TMD of 8C-8A(IL125).
source: As shown in Figure 7A, we observe non-protein densities penetrating through the openings between the subunits in the TMD.
evidence: This is an observation from the cryo-EM structure shown in Figure 7A.

claim: The shape and length of the non-protein densities between subunits are consistent with lipid molecules.
source: The shape and length of these densities are consistent with lipid molecules.
evidence: This is an inference based on the characteristics of the observed densities.

claim: Similar lipid-like densities are observed in LRRC8A hexameric channels reconstituted in lipid nanodiscs.
source: Similar densities are observed in LRRC8A hexameric channels reconstituted in lipid nanodiscs (Kern et al., 2019).
evidence: This is a comparison to a previous structural study.

claim: Lipid-like densities are observed on both the cytoplasmic and extracellular sides of the TMD in 8C-8A(IL125).
source: We observe these lipid-like densities on both the cytoplasmic and extracellular sides of the TMD.
evidence: This is an observation from the cryo-EM structure.

claim: The lipid-like density closer to the intracellular side is considerably weaker at the loose interfaces compared to the tight interfaces.
source: However, the lipid-like density closer to the intracellular side is considerably weaker at the loose interfaces compared to the ones at the tight interfaces (Figure 7A).
evidence: This is an observation from the cryo-EM structure shown in Figure 7A.

claim: The weaker lipid-like density at loose interfaces may be due to the larger separation of the subunits, creating more room for lipid molecules to move.
source: This difference may be due to the larger separation of the subunits at the loose interface, creating more room for the lipid molecules to move.
evidence: This is speculation about the cause of the observed density differences.

claim: The lipid-like densities with the strongest features suggest phospholipids as the most likely candidates.
source: Although the quality of the maps does not allow us to identify the lipid molecules leading to the densities we observe, the ones with the strongest features suggest phospholipids as the most likely candidates (Figure 7B).
evidence: This is an inference based on the characteristics of the observed densities shown in Figure 7B.

claim: A phospholipid molecule can be reasonably fitted into the strongest lipid-like density.
source: As shown in Figure 7B, a phospholipid molecule can be reasonably fitted into the strongest density we observe.
evidence: This is a modeling result shown in Figure 7B.

claim: The polar phosphate moiety of the lipid molecule is coordinated by K125, K318, and H314 of neighboring subunits.
source: The polar phosphate moiety of the lipid molecule is coordinated by two lysine residues (K125 and K318) and a histidine residue (H314) of the neighboring subunits (Figure 7B).
evidence: This is a structural observation from the modeled lipid shown in Figure 7B.

claim: W122, Y126, and L130 are close to the acyl chains of the modeled lipid.
source: W122, Y126, and L130 are close to the acyl chains (Figure 7B).
evidence: This is a structural observation from the modeled lipid shown in Figure 7B.

claim: One of the acyl chains of the modeled lipid extends through the space between the subunit and reaches the interior surface of the channel.
source: One of the acyl chains extends through the space between the subunit and reaches the interior surface of the channel.
evidence: This is a structural observation from the modeled lipid.

claim: The pore-lining residues have high densities of charged amino acid residues that align with the phospholipid head groups of the membrane bilayer.
source: When we examined the surface properties of the pore-lining residues, we found high densities of charged amino acid residues that align with the phospholipid head groups of the membrane bilayer surrounding the TMD (Figure 7C).
evidence: This is a structural observation from the analysis shown in Figure 7C.

claim: A hydrophobic patch of amino acid residues aligns with the hydrophobic core of the membrane bilayer.
source: A hydrophobic patch of amino acid residues aligns with the hydrophobic core of the membrane bilayer (Figure 7D).
evidence: This is a structural observation from the analysis shown in Figure 7D.

claim: Two layers of non-protein densities are observed within the channel pore that align with the boundaries of the hydrophobic patch and the detergent micelle.
source: Intriguingly, we observed two layers of non-protein densities within the channel pore that align with the boundaries of the hydrophobic patch and the detergent micelle around the TMD in the cryo-EM maps for all classes (Figure 7E).
evidence: This is an observation from the cryo-EM structure shown in Figure 7E.

claim: Similar pore-blocking densities have been observed in the structures of other large-pore channels, including pannexins and innexin.
source: Similar densities have been observed in the structures of other large-pore channels, including pannexins and innexin (Burendei et al., 2020; Kuzuya et al., 2022).
evidence: This is a comparison to previous structural studies.

claim: The pore-blocking densities are plausibly a lipid bilayer that occupies the pore.
source: It is plausible that these densities are of a lipid bilayer that occupies the pore as illustrated in Figure 7F.
evidence: This is speculation based on the observed densities, illustrated in Figure 7F.

claim: The same bilayer-like density within the channel pore was visible in 8C-8A(IL125) reconstituted in lipid nanodiscs.
source: To confirm that these densities are not detergent-induced artifacts, we reconstituted the 8C-8A(IL125) chimera in lipid nanodiscs and performed cryo-EM analysis (Figure 7—figure supplement 1). Although the resolution of the cryo-EM maps could not be improved beyond 7 Å, the same bilayer-like density within the channel pore was visible (Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is an observation from the nanodisc cryo-EM structure shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: The lipid-like densities within the pores are similar in intensity and shape to the lipid densities observed around the protein within the nanodisc.
source: It is noteworthy that the lipid-like densities within the pores are similar in intensity and shape to the lipid densities observed around the protein within the nanodisc (Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is an observation from the nanodisc cryo-EM structure shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: Homomeric LRRC8 channels other than LRRC8A do not traffic to the plasma membrane.
source: Except for LRRC8A, homomeric LRRC8 channels do not traffic to the plasma membrane and cannot be functionally characterized (Voss et al., 2014; Yamada and Strange, 2018; Zhou et al., 2018).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: LRRC8A homomers form plasma membrane channels.
source: LRRC8A homomers form plasma membrane channels, but they exhibit abnormal functional properties.
evidence: This is established knowledge.

claim: LRRC8A channels are not activated by cell swelling under normal physiological conditions.
source: Most notably, LRRC8A channels are not activated by cell swelling under normal physiological conditions (Yamada et al., 2021; Yamada and Strange, 2018) and are only weakly activated by extreme reductions in cytoplasmic ionic strength (Figure 6—figure supplement 1; Yamada et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citations and data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: LRRC8A channels are only weakly activated by extreme reductions in cytoplasmic ionic strength.
source: Most notably, LRRC8A channels are not activated by cell swelling under normal physiological conditions (Yamada et al., 2021; Yamada and Strange, 2018) and are only weakly activated by extreme reductions in cytoplasmic ionic strength (Figure 6—figure supplement 1; Yamada et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citations and data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: LRRC8A channels exhibit grossly abnormal DCPIB pharmacology.
source: LRRC8A channels also exhibit grossly abnormal DCPIB pharmacology (Yamada et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citation.

claim: The non-native functional properties of LRRC8A channels indicate that they have a non-native structure.
source: The non-native functional properties of LRRC8A channels indicate that they have a non-native structure, which presents significant limitations for understanding how VRAC/LRRC8 channels are regulated and how pore structure determines solute permeability characteristics.
evidence: This is an inference based on the abnormal functional properties.

claim: 8C-8A(IL125) chimeric channels exhibit normal sensitivity to cell volume changes.
source: The 8C-8A(IL125) chimeric channel exhibits normal sensitivity to cell volume changes and intracellular ionic strength and normal DCPIB pharmacology (Figure 6—figure supplement 1; Yamada et al., 2021; Yamada and Strange, 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations and data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: 8C-8A(IL125) chimeric channels exhibit normal sensitivity to intracellular ionic strength.
source: The 8C-8A(IL125) chimeric channel exhibits normal sensitivity to cell volume changes and intracellular ionic strength and normal DCPIB pharmacology (Figure 6—figure supplement 1; Yamada et al., 2021; Yamada and Strange, 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations and data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: The number of subunits required to form native VRAC/LRRC8 channels is unknown.
source: The number of subunits required to form native VRAC/LRRC8 channels is unknown.
evidence: This reflects current knowledge about VRAC stoichiometry.

claim: Native gel, crosslinking, and mass spectrometry studies suggest that VRAC/LRRC8 channels are formed by ≥6 LRRC8 subunits.
source: However, native gel, crosslinking, and mass spectrometry studies (Syeda et al., 2016) and photobleaching experiments (Gaitán-Peñas et al., 2016) suggest that VRAC/LRRC8 channels are formed by ≥6 LRRC8 subunits.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Photobleaching experiments suggest that VRAC/LRRC8 channels are formed by ≥6 LRRC8 subunits.
source: However, native gel, crosslinking, and mass spectrometry studies (Syeda et al., 2016) and photobleaching experiments (Gaitán-Peñas et al., 2016) suggest that VRAC/LRRC8 channels are formed by ≥6 LRRC8 subunits.
evidence: This is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: The 8C-8A(IL125) limiting pore radius of 4.7 Å is very consistent with the 6–7 Å pore radius estimated for native VRAC/LRRC8 channels.
source: The 8C-8A(IL125) has a limiting pore radius of 4.7 Å (Figure 6 and Figure 6—figure supplement 2A), which unlike the much narrower LRRC8A pore (Figure 6 and Figure 6—figure supplement 2B), is very consistent with the 6–7 Å pore radius estimated for native VRAC/LRRC8 channels (Droogmans et al., 1999; Ternovsky et al., 2004) and the role of these channels play in the transport of large anionic and uncharged organic solutes (Sabirov and Okada, 2005; Strange et al., 2019).
evidence: This is a comparison of structural measurements to literature values.

claim: Native VRAC/LRRC8 channels have an estimated pore radius of 6–7 Å.
source: The 8C-8A(IL125) has a limiting pore radius of 4.7 Å (Figure 6 and Figure 6—figure supplement 2A), which unlike the much narrower LRRC8A pore (Figure 6 and Figure 6—figure supplement 2B), is very consistent with the 6–7 Å pore radius estimated for native VRAC/LRRC8 channels (Droogmans et al., 1999; Ternovsky et al., 2004) and the role of these channels play in the transport of large anionic and uncharged organic solutes (Sabirov and Okada, 2005; Strange et al., 2019).
evidence: This is established knowledge from previous studies.

claim: A leucine residue at position 105 forms the 8C-8A(IL125) pore constriction.
source: A leucine residue located at position 105 forms the 8C-8A(IL125) pore constriction (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is a structural observation shown in Figure 6A.

claim: In LRRC8A and LRRC8B, L105 is replaced by arginine.
source: In LRRC8A and LRRC8B, L105 is replaced by arginine.
evidence: This is a sequence comparison.

claim: LRRC8D and LRRC8E paralogs have either phenylalanine or leucine at the position homologous to L105.
source: LRRC8D and LRRC8E paralogs have either phenylalanine or leucine at the homologous position.
evidence: This is a sequence comparison.

claim: Hexameric LRRC8A channels have a limiting pore radius of 2.0 Å.
source: Hexameric LRRC8A and LRRC8D channels have limiting pore radii of 2.0 and 3.5 Å, respectively (Figure 6B and Figure 6—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is a measurement from structural analysis shown in Figure 6.

claim: Hexameric LRRC8D channels have a limiting pore radius of 3.5 Å.
source: Hexameric LRRC8A and LRRC8D channels have limiting pore radii of 2.0 and 3.5 Å, respectively (Figure 6B and Figure 6—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is a measurement from structural analysis shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2.

claim: When hypothetical heptamers are created by aligning LRRC8A subunits onto individual 8C-8A(IL125) subunits, the pore radius increases to 4.7 Å.
source: When we create hypothetical heptamers by aligning LRRC8A and LRRC8D subunits onto individual 8C-8A(IL125) subunits, the pore radii increase to 4.7 and 7.1 Å, respectively, indicating that the oligomeric state has a direct impact in pore size and likely in channel transport properties (Figure 6—figure supplement 2D–F).
evidence: This is a modeling result shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2.

claim: When hypothetical heptamers are created by aligning LRRC8D subunits onto individual 8C-8A(IL125) subunits, the pore radius increases to 7.1 Å.
source: When we create hypothetical heptamers by aligning LRRC8A and LRRC8D subunits onto individual 8C-8A(IL125) subunits, the pore radii increase to 4.7 and 7.1 Å, respectively, indicating that the oligomeric state has a direct impact in pore size and likely in channel transport properties (Figure 6—figure supplement 2D–F).
evidence: This is a modeling result shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2.

claim: The oligomeric state has a direct impact on pore size.
source: When we create hypothetical heptamers by aligning LRRC8A and LRRC8D subunits onto individual 8C-8A(IL125) subunits, the pore radii increase to 4.7 and 7.1 Å, respectively, indicating that the oligomeric state has a direct impact in pore size and likely in channel transport properties (Figure 6—figure supplement 2D–F).
evidence: This is an inference based on the modeling results.

claim: The oligomeric state likely impacts channel transport properties.
source: When we create hypothetical heptamers by aligning LRRC8A and LRRC8D subunits onto individual 8C-8A(IL125) subunits, the pore radii increase to 4.7 and 7.1 Å, respectively, indicating that the oligomeric state has a direct impact in pore size and likely in channel transport properties (Figure 6—figure supplement 2D–F).
evidence: This is an inference based on the modeling results.

claim: The narrow pore radius of 2 Å of the LRRC8A hexameric channel likely accounts for its abnormal DCPIB pharmacology.
source: The narrow pore radius of 2 Å of the LRRC8A hexameric channel (Figure 6B) also likely accounts for its abnormal DCPIB pharmacology.
evidence: This is an inference connecting structural and functional properties.

claim: Native VRAC/LRRC8 channels are inhibited >90% by 10 μM DCPIB.
source: Native VRAC/LRRC8 channels are inhibited >90% by 10 μM DCPIB.
evidence: This is established knowledge about native channel pharmacology.

claim: DCPIB inhibition of native VRAC/LRRC8 channels is voltage-insensitive.
source: Inhibition is voltage-insensitive and exhibits a Hill coefficient of 2.9 (Friard et al., 2017), suggesting that multiple DCPIB molecules are required to inhibit the channel.
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: DCPIB inhibition of native VRAC/LRRC8 channels exhibits a Hill coefficient of 2.9.
source: Inhibition is voltage-insensitive and exhibits a Hill coefficient of 2.9 (Friard et al., 2017), suggesting that multiple DCPIB molecules are required to inhibit the channel.
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: Multiple DCPIB molecules are required to inhibit native VRAC/LRRC8 channels.
source: Inhibition is voltage-insensitive and exhibits a Hill coefficient of 2.9 (Friard et al., 2017), suggesting that multiple DCPIB molecules are required to inhibit the channel.
evidence: This is an inference based on the Hill coefficient.

claim: The DCPIB pharmacology of 8C-8A(IL125) recapitulates that of native VRAC/LRRC8 channels.
source: The DCPIB pharmacology of 8C-8A(IL125) recapitulates that of native VRAC/LRRC8 channels (Yamada et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citation.

claim: LRRC8A hexameric channels are weakly inhibited by 10 μM DCPIB.
source: In contrast, LRRC8A hexameric channels are weakly inhibited by 10 μM DCPIB, and inhibition is strongly voltage-dependent with a Hill coefficient close to 1 (Yamada et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citation.

claim: DCPIB inhibition of LRRC8A hexameric channels is strongly voltage-dependent.
source: In contrast, LRRC8A hexameric channels are weakly inhibited by 10 μM DCPIB, and inhibition is strongly voltage-dependent with a Hill coefficient close to 1 (Yamada et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citation.

claim: DCPIB inhibition of LRRC8A hexameric channels has a Hill coefficient close to 1.
source: In contrast, LRRC8A hexameric channels are weakly inhibited by 10 μM DCPIB, and inhibition is strongly voltage-dependent with a Hill coefficient close to 1 (Yamada et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citation.

claim: The low Hill coefficient for DCPIB inhibition of LRRC8A is consistent with a single DCPIB molecule blocking the channel pore.
source: The low Hill coefficient is consistent with an LRRC8A cryo-EM structure described by Kern et al., 2019, showing a single DCPIB molecule blocking the channel pore at the narrowest constriction formed by R103 (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is an inference connecting functional and structural data.

claim: A cryo-EM structure shows a single DCPIB molecule blocking the LRRC8A channel pore at the narrowest constriction formed by R103.
source: The low Hill coefficient is consistent with an LRRC8A cryo-EM structure described by Kern et al., 2019, showing a single DCPIB molecule blocking the channel pore at the narrowest constriction formed by R103 (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is a description of a previous structural study.

claim: Two recent studies have defined high-resolution cryo-EM structures of LRRC8A/LRRC8C heteromeric channels.
source: Two recent studies have defined high-resolution cryo-EM structures of LRRC8A/LRRC8C heteromeric channels (Kern et al., 2022; Rutz et al., 2023).
evidence: This is a reference to recent structural studies.

claim: LRRC8A/LRRC8C heteromeric channels can adopt a hexameric conformation with a limiting pore radius of 2–3 Å.
source: Both studies demonstrated that the heteromeric channels could adopt a hexameric conformation with a limiting pore radius of 2–3 Å, similar to that of LRRC8A hexamers.
evidence: This is a summary of findings from recent structural studies.

claim: LRRC8A/LRRC8C heteromers can have 5:1 LRRC8A:LRRC8C stoichiometry.
source: However, these channels either had 5:1 (Kern et al., 2022) or 4:2 LRRC8A:LRRC8C stoichiometries, indicating that LRRC8A:LRRC8C heteromers can adopt multiple oligomeric forms.
evidence: This is a finding from a recent structural study.

claim: LRRC8A/LRRC8C heteromers can have 4:2 LRRC8A:LRRC8C stoichiometry.
source: However, these channels either had 5:1 (Kern et al., 2022) or 4:2 LRRC8A:LRRC8C stoichiometries, indicating that LRRC8A:LRRC8C heteromers can adopt multiple oligomeric forms.
evidence: This is a finding from a recent structural study.

claim: LRRC8A:LRRC8C heteromers can adopt multiple oligomeric forms.
source: However, these channels either had 5:1 (Kern et al., 2022) or 4:2 LRRC8A:LRRC8C stoichiometries, indicating that LRRC8A:LRRC8C heteromers can adopt multiple oligomeric forms.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observed stoichiometric variability.

claim: Native VRAC/LRRC8 channels may exist in multiple oligomeric conformations.
source: Taken together, existing cryo-EM structural data suggest that native VRAC/LRRC8 channels may exist in multiple oligomeric conformations, as has been reported for CALHM channels.
evidence: This is speculation based on the current and previous structural data.

claim: Four groups have shown that LRRC8A has a dominant-negative function.
source: Four groups have shown that LRRC8A has a dominant-negative function.
evidence: This is a summary of findings from multiple studies.

claim: Overexpression of LRRC8A suppresses endogenous VRAC/LRRC8 currents.
source: Overexpression of LRRC8A suppresses endogenous (Qiu et al., 2014; Syeda et al., 2016; Voss et al., 2014) and heterologously expressed (Yamada et al., 2016) VRAC/LRRC8 currents.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Overexpression of LRRC8A suppresses heterologously expressed VRAC/LRRC8 currents.
source: Overexpression of LRRC8A suppresses endogenous (Qiu et al., 2014; Syeda et al., 2016; Voss et al., 2014) and heterologously expressed (Yamada et al., 2016) VRAC/LRRC8 currents.
evidence: This is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: LRRC8A protein levels may impact channel assembly and function.
source: LRRC8A protein levels may therefore impact channel assembly and function.
evidence: This is an inference based on the dominant-negative function of LRRC8A.

claim: Kern et al. identified lipids located between individual subunits in LRRC8A hexameric channels reconstituted in lipid nanodiscs.
source: Kern et al. identified lipids located between individual subunits in LRRC8A hexameric channels reconstituted in lipid nanodiscs (Kern et al., 2019).
evidence: This is a reference to a previous structural study.

claim: In a recent pre-print reporting the hexameric structure of LRRC8A-LRRC8C, ordered lipid molecules are observed on the extracellular side of the pore opening.
source: In agreement with our observations, in a recent pre-print reporting the hexameric structure of LRRC8A-LRRC8C (Kern et al., 2022), ordered lipid molecules are observed on the extracellular side of the pore opening aligning well with the densities we observed.
evidence: This is a reference to a recent pre-print study.

claim: Intrapore lipids have been proposed to be critical structural and regulatory elements of pannexins.
source: Intrapore lipids have recently been proposed to be critical structural and regulatory elements of pannexins (Kuzuya et al., 2022) and closely related innexin (Burendei et al., 2020) and CALHM (Drożdżyk et al., 2020; Syrjanen et al., 2020) channels, as well as bacterial mechanosensitive channels (Rasmussen et al., 2019; Reddy et al., 2019; Zhang et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citations to recent studies.

claim: Intrapore lipids have been proposed to be critical structural and regulatory elements of innexin channels.
source: Intrapore lipids have recently been proposed to be critical structural and regulatory elements of pannexins (Kuzuya et al., 2022) and closely related innexin (Burendei et al., 2020) and CALHM (Drożdżyk et al., 2020; Syrjanen et al., 2020) channels, as well as bacterial mechanosensitive channels (Rasmussen et al., 2019; Reddy et al., 2019; Zhang et al., 2021).
